case_name: Children’s Aid Society of Sudbury and Manitoulin v. S.(T.)
text:
WARNING

The court hearing this matter directs
that the following notice should be attached to the file:

This
is a case under Part III of the
Child and Family Services Act
and is
subject to subsections 48(7), 45(8) and 45(9) of the Act.
These subsections and
subsection 85(3)

of the
Child and Family Services Act
,
which deals with the consequences of failure to
comply, read as follows:

45.—
(7)
Order
excluding media representatives or prohibiting publication.
—   The
court may make an order,

.  .  .

(
c
)

prohibiting the publication of a report
of the hearing or a specified part of the hearing,

where the court is of the opinion that
. . .  the publication of the report,
. . ., would cause emotional harm to a child who is a witness
at or a participant in the hearing or is the subject of the proceeding.

(8)
Prohibition: identifying child.—
No
person shall publish or make public information that has the effect of
identifying a child who is a witness at or a participant in a hearing or the
subject of a proceeding, or the child's parent or foster parent or a member
of the child's family.

(9)
Idem: order re
adult.
—   The court may make an order prohibiting the publication
of information that has the effect of identifying a person charged with an offence
under this Part.

.   .   .

85.
—(3)
Idem.
—   A
person who contravenes subsection 45(8) (publication of identifying
information) or an order prohibiting publication made under clause 45(7)(
c
)
or subsection 45(9), and a director, officer or employee of a corporation who
authorizes, permits or concurs in such a contravention by the corporation, is
guilty of an offence and on conviction is liable to a fine of not more than
$10,000 or to imprisonment for a term of not more than three years, or to
both.

Sudbury Registry
No. C-611-05

DATE:   2009·II·06

CITATION:
Children’s Aid
Society of
Sudbury
and Manitoulin v. S.(T.)
, 2009 ONCJ 70

ONTARIO
COURT  OF  JUSTICE

BETWEEN:

CHILDREN’S  AID  SOCIETY
OF  THE  DISTRICTS  OF  SUDBURY  AND  MANITOULIN,

Applicant,

—  AND  —

T.S.,  P.T.,  MOOSE  CREE
FIRST  NATION  and  ATTAWAPISKAT  FIRST  NATION,

Respondents.

Before Justice John D. Keast

Heard on 10-12
and 25 September 2008; and 31 October 2008

Reasons for
Judgment released on 6 February 2009

CHILD PROTECTION — Form of order — Crown
wardship — Grounds — Likelihood of change in circumstances — Children’s aid
society had intervened because of parenting deficits, substance abuse issues
and domestic violence — Two oldest children (now 4 and 2¾ years old) had been
in society care for past 2½ years — Youngest child (now 9 months old) had been
in care since birth — On matters of parenting deficits and the substance abuse,
mother had made considerable progress to society’s satisfaction — On issue of
domestic violence, society told mother to terminate her relationship with
violent and abusive partner (children’s father) before children could be
returned — Unfortunately, court’s review of social science literature on domestic
violence suggested that this mother had features commonly referred to as
“battered wife syndrome” where she would flee from partner’s abuse and even lay
charges only to return to him and drop any charges — Despite history of such
abuse, she repeatedly seemed to choose this him over children and both he and
she ignored “no contact” provisions in court orders and terms of bail and
probation — Less than year ago, she was pleading against father’s imprisonment
at his criminal sentencing hearing with view to their reconciliation — And on
eve of status review, she had actually allowed father to stay at her residence
— At that status review hearing, however, she presented plan for children’s
return to her under terms and conditions of 12-month supervision order, promising
to abide by “no contact” order
vis-à-vis
father and to co-operate
completely with society — Court found it unreasonable to expect that father
would stay away from mother and found it unrealistic to expect immediate
termination of contact between parents who had, over long time developed casual
and comfortable relationship wherein they had little if any concern about
breaching probation orders — Moreover, mother had only recently started
domestic violence counselling where it appeared that domestic violence issue
was deep-rooted and longstanding, complicated by other underlying psychological
factors for which extensive therapy was required, probably for indefinite and
lengthy period and for which her prognosis was unknown and  essentially
conjecture — Thus, at this time, risks from domestic violence remained high,
unlikely to be reduced soon and supervision order (as proposed in mother’s
plan) was simply not designed to manage risk of such high level — Mother’s plan
needed to show some basis for court to find that she would be able to parent
children without unreasonably endangering their safety, but that did not exist
in this case — In meantime, children’s lives could no longer be put on hold in
hopes that mother might be rehabilitated — Crown wardship for the three
children.

STATUTES AND REGULATIONS CITED

Child and Family Services Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-11 [as amended],
subclause 37(2)
(
b
)(i),

subclause 37(2)
(
b
)(ii),
subsection 37(3)
and
subsection 59(2)
.

CASES CITED

Children’s
Aid Society of Algoma v. P. (Deborah) and L. (Henry)
,
2006 ONCJ 170
, 28 R.F.L. (6th) 372, [2006] O.J. No. 1878, 2006
Cars­well­Ont 2974 (Ont. C.J.).

Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. C. (Sheila Ann)
,
[2005] O.J. No. 2154, 143 A.C.W.S. (3d) 869, [2005] W.D.F.L. 3688,
2005 ONCJ
274
, 2005 Cars­well­Ont 2424 (Ont. C.J.); affirmed at
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. C. (Sheila Ann)
,
2005 CanLII 43289
, 143
A.C.W.S. 3d 510, [2005] O.J. No. 4718, 2005 Cars­well­Ont 5932 (Ont. S.C.);
further affirmed at
Children's
Aid Society of Toronto v. C. (Sheila Ann)
,
2007
ONCA 474
, 158 A.C.W.S. (3d) 610, [2007] W.D.F.L. 2844, [2007] O.J. No.
2609, 2007 Cars­well­Ont 4267 (Ont. C.A.); permission to appeal to the Supreme
Court of Canada refused at
C.
(Sheila Ann) v. Children's Aid Society of Toronto
, [2007] 3 S.C.R.
xiv
,

2007 CanLII 66780
, [2007] S.C.C.A. No. 462, 2007 Cars­well­Ont 7859.

Jewish
Family and Child Service of Toronto v. K. (Rachel), K. (Tamara) and T. (Edward
King)
,
2008 ONCJ 774
, [2008] O.J. No. 1940,
[2008] O.J. No. 5856, 2008 Cars­well­Ont 9306 (Ont. C.J.).

Roy A. Sullivan  ..............................................................................   counsel
for the applicant society

Helen Florentis  ..................................................................   counsel
for the respondent mother, T.S.

No appearance by or on behalf of the
respondent father, P.T., even though served with notice

No appearance by or on behalf of the
Moose Cree First Nation, even though served with notice

No appearance by or on behalf of the
Attawapiskat First Nation, even though served with notice

JUSTICE J.D. KEAST:—

1:     NATURE OF THE APPLICATION

[
1
]

This is an application by way of status
review for Crown wardship without access in relation to the three children,
namely, T.T. (born on 22 January 2005. age 4 years), L.T. (born on 21 April
2006, age 2 years, 9 months) and S.T.C. (born on 4 April 2008, age 9 months).
The mother is 24 years old and the father 26 years old.  The parents and children
are status Indians.  The father and the two bands did not participate in this proceeding.

[
2
]

The two older children have been in care
since 1 August 2006, for a total of two years and three months at the
conclusion of the trial.  The youngest child has been in care since birth,
being 4 April 2008.

2:     HISTORY OF THE PROCEEDING

[
3
]

The following is a history of the
proceedings:

(a)

15 November 2005
— interim order placing T.T. in the care of the parents pursuant
to terms and conditions of supervision;

(b)

2 May 2006
— further interim order to include the newborn child, L.T. in the
interim supervision order;

(c)

20 June 2006
— a finding was made that the children T.T. and L.T. are in need
of protection and a final six month supervision order was granted.  The
finding was based on the risk of physical harm pursuant to
subclause 37(2)
(
b
)(i)
of the
Child and Family Services Act
, R.S.O. 1990, c. C-11, as amended
(hereinafter referred to as the “Act”).  The factual basis for the finding
was parenting deficits of both parents, substance abuse of both parents and
domestic violence from the father to the mother.

(d)

August 1, 2006
— the society apprehended the two children and requested a
six-month society wardship order.  An interim wardship order was granted
leaving the children in the care of the society;

(e)

17 November 2006
— a six-month society wardship order was granted with respect to
the two children;

(f)

8 May 2007
— the society requested a Crown wardship order with no access in
relation to the two children.

(g)

4 April 2008
— The youngest child, S.T.C., was apprehended at birth from the
hospital.  An interim order placing the child in the care of the society was
granted on 8 April 2008.

(h)

8 April 2008
— A further status review application was brought in relation to
the newborn child, requesting Crown wardship with no access.

[
4
]

Initially, the primary risk factors were
parenting deficits, substance abuse issues and domestic violence.  However, the
mother has made considerable progress dealing with parenting deficits and the
substance abuse issue.  For the most part, since the spring of 2007, except for
one known relapse, the mother has remained free from the use of drugs and alcohol.
She has made substantial improvements in her parenting.  She has received substance
abuse therapy and has taken parenting programs.

[
5
]

The one remaining risk issue is domestic
violence.  The society has made it clear since the spring of 2007 that, if the
children were to be returned to the mother, she must terminate the relationship
with the father.  As the mother made substantial progress in the areas of parenting
and substance abuse, the society continued to advise her that the most significant
factor for herself and the children was the domestic violence from the father
to herself.  If the father did not exist or if the relationship was clearly
terminated, the society would have returned the children to the mother.

3:     DOMESTIC VIOLENCE

3.1:     General

[
6
]

In order to assess the risk to the children
occasioned by domestic violence, I must examine the history and dynamics of the
relationship between the mother and father.  The relationship was volatile,
chaotic and unstable.  There were repeated assaults by the father on the
mother.  On three occasions, he was convicted of common or simple assault.
There were other assaults that did not lead to criminal charges.

[
7
]

The mother displayed features of what is
commonly referred to as the “battered wife syndrome”.  She would complain to
the police and then attempt to prevent charges from being processed.  She has
refused to give statements after an initial complaint.  On a bail hearing, she
supported his being released pending trial.  She supported him in his criminal
sentence hearings and did not want him incarcerated.  She made several promises
to terminate the relationship but went back to him.  She has said that she
cannot raise children without him.  She has minimized his behaviour and risks
to herself and the children.  At importance junctures, she has chosen him over
the children.  At least twice, she has fled to a home for female victims of
domestic violence, only to reconcile with him.

3.2:     History of Assaults

[
8
]

The first known assault took place a few
days before the birth of the first child, being 22 January 2005.  No charges
were laid.

[
9
]

Another assault took place on 11 February
2005, some three weeks after the birth of the oldest child.  There was an
argument and altercation.  The father punched the mother in the nose with
sufficient force to bloody the nose.  During the struggle, the father stepped
on the baby’s foot but the baby was not hurt.  The father had been drinking.
The mother insisted that the charges be dropped so that the father could help
out more at home.  The father was convicted on 2 March 2005, was given a
suspended sentence and placed on probation.  Among the terms was a
non-association and non-communication restriction with the mother.

[
10
]

On 14 October 2005, a heated argument took
place between the parents.  Fearful of the argument escalating, the mother fled
to Genevra House.  She took the baby with her.  After staying for a few days,
she reconciled with the father.

[
11
]

On January 26, 2006, the society received a
call from the police reporting a domestic dispute.  The call was initiated by
the mother.  The police expressed concern about the safety of the child T.T.
and the mother was reluctant to leave the residence.  She eventually did leave
the residence and attended at Genevra House.  The mother indicated an argument
ensued and the father pushed her to her knees.  The father hit her in the nose,
twice tried to choke her and shook her.  The mother threw a DVD player at the
father.  The child T.T. was present and was afraid.  When the father left the
residence, he took the telephone cord.  The mother had to leave the residence
to find a payphone to call the police.  When the police requested a statement,
she refused to participate in the statement process.  She indicated that the
father might go to jail and not be present for the second child’s birth.  No
charges were laid.

[
12
]

A few days later, while the mother was still
at Genevra House, she advised the social worker she wanted to reconcile with
the father.  After discussions, the mother agreed to hold off on
reconciliation, but a short time later, she insisted that she wanted to reconcile.

[
13
]

A further assault occurred on 30 July 2006.
The mother called police who in turn called the society.  The parents had been
drinking and an argument ensued as to the amount of time that the father was
spending with the children.  The father punched the mother twice in the side of
the head.  She called an ambulance and attended hospital.  The police observed
other bruises on the mother’s arms, which were consistent with her arms being
forcefully grabbed.

[
14
]

The two children were apprehended and have
been in care since.

[
15
]

After initially providing information to the
police as to what happened, the mother would not provide details to the social
worker conducting the investigation.  Charges were laid against the father.

[
16
]

At the subsequent bail hearing, the mother
was present in court and was communicating directly with the father.  The
father was released on bail wherein one of the terms and conditions was a “no
communication” order with the mother.  The mother advised the Crown and the
court that she wants to regain custody of her children and to reconcile with
the father.

[
17
]

On 1 October 2006, the father pleaded guilty
to assault and was placed on probation for 24 months.  There was a condition he
not communicate directly or indirectly with the mother.  He also had to
participate in a domestic abuse therapy program.

[
18
]

On 21 January 2007, the mother and father
had an altercation on a public street.  There was arguing but not assaultive
behaviour.  The police intervened.  This communication was contrary to the
probation order.

[
19
]

On 21 December 2007, the father slapped the
mother and pushed her to the ground.  At the time, the mother was five months
pregnant for the youngest child.  He pleaded guilty to assault and was
ultimately sentenced on 21 April 2008.  The previous “no contact” order, which
existed in prior probation orders, was modified to allow the mother and father
to communicate with each other by telephone only and in public places on
Mondays, Thursdays and Saturdays between 1:00 p.m. and 5:00 p.m. or other times
with the written permission of the probation officer.  The mother cancelled her
access visit with the three children on the morning of 21 April 2008 in order
to attend the sentence hearing.  The court was advised that the couple wished
to reconcile and to resume cohabitation at some point.

[
20
]

On 15 February 2008, the father’s probation
officer was at the bus depot.  The father was leaving on the bus and was saying
goodbye to the mother.  This was a breach of the “no contact” order.  It is the
opinion of the probation officer there have been many breaches of the “no
contact” order.

3.3:     The Timmins Incident

[
21
]

There is an alleged assault by the father
against the mother in mid June 2008.  Because of the significance of this
incident, the analysis of which will be dealt with later, I will review the
details surrounding the incident.

[
22
]

The father is employed for a diamond mine
near Attawapiskat, Ontario, in
proximity to James Bay.  He
works in rotating block periods of time.  When he is not working, he then
spends block periods of time in Sudbury, Ontario.  He provides the society with his block periods of
employment and the periods of time when he is at his residence in Sudbury, so that the society can schedule
his supervised access with the children.  Transportation to Attawapiskat
involves a bus between Sudbury
and Timmins, Ontario and then
an air flight between Timmins and Attawapiskat.  This is reversed on his way back to Sudbury.

[
23
]

The father advised the society he would be
in Sudbury between 11 and 23
June 2008 and requested the society to set up his supervised access with the
children during this period.

[
24
]

The mother advised the society she would be
in Timmins, Ontario visiting
her sister and would not be available for visits with the children until 12
June 2008.  The society was provided with this information in the early morning
of 9 June 2008.  As a result, some visits had to be cancelled.  It was expected
that the mother would be back in Sudbury to proceed with her visit of 12 June 2008.

[
25
]

The mother is now in Timmins between 9 and 11 June 2008.  The
father is expected to travel through Timmins on 10 June 2008 in order to be back in Sudbury for 11 June 2008.  However, on 10 June 2008, the father left a
voice mail with the social worker indicating he would not be in Sudbury until
13 June 2008 because he had to stay in Attawapiskat and to work for a few extra days.

[
26
]

On 12 June 2008, the mother was not at her
residence when the children were brought over for the regularly scheduled
access visit.  The mother did not call the society to inform that she would not
be present.  As per the initial indication, she was to be back from Timmins in time for the visit of 12 June
2008 with the children.

[
27
]

On 16 June 2008, the social worker attended
the mother’s residence and observed the mother to have a black left eye.  On
inquiry, the mother advised she was in the downtown area of Timmins with her sister and became involved
in an argument with her sister’s boyfriend.  The mother alleges that the
boyfriend punched her in the face.  The mother refused to provide the social
worker with the name of the boyfriend.  Because of the suspicious circumstances
wherein it appears that the mother and father were in Timmins together, the social worker suggested to the mother that she was
together with the father.  The mother strongly denied this suggestion.  The
mother was asked why she did not make the visit of 12 June 2008 with the
children in Sudbury or call to
cancel the visit and she responded she had missed her bus.

[
28
]

By now, the social worker was suspicious
that the mother and father were together in Timmins and it was the father who assaulted the mother.  On 16 June 2008,
the social worker spoke with the father who insisted his work period was
extended and this was the reason for the delay in travelling back to Sudbury.  The social worker requested the
father to sign a consent to allow her to speak to the employer or to obtain a
letter indicating the father extended his work time.  The father indicated that
he would obtain a letter.  No letter has been forthcoming.  The society alleges
that it was not the sister’s boyfriend who assaulted the mother; it was likely
the father.  If the mother and father were together in Timmins, it would be a breach of the father’s probation order of 21 April
2008.

3.4:     Post 21 April 2008 Breaches

[
29
]

The criminal court was impressed with the
presentation on behalf of the father (and the mother) during the sentence
hearing of 21 April 2008.  The court made a decision to allow limited contact
between the mother and father, three days a week between the hours of 1:00 p.m.
and 5:00 p.m. and only in public places.  This was in recognition of the very
strong desire of the mother and father to reconcile and eventually to
re-cohabit.  But this was not enough.  They continued to see each other outside
of the permissible time periods.

[
30
]

On 26 August 2008, there was a scheduled
visit at the mother’s residence from 9:00 a.m. to 1:00 p.m.  The social worker
usually arrives with the children at 9:00 a.m.  On this particular day, she
arrived 15 minutes early.  She observed the father leaving the residence and at
the same time pulling a toque over his head.  His movements appeared evasive to
the social worker.  The father’s attendance at her residence was clearly a
breach of the probation order of 21 April 2008.

[
31
]

On 8 September 2008, a social worker from
the society attended a medical walk-in clinic at 7:20 p.m.  She observed the
mother and father sitting together in the waiting room.  The social worker
spoke with the mother then the father left the clinic.  This was a breach of
the probation order of 21 April 2008.

[
32
]

Since the probation order of 21 April 2008,
as well as before, the mother has attended with the father at many Alcoholics
Anonymous meetings.  These take place at night.  These communications are also
a breach of the probation order of 21 April 2008.

3.5:     Social Science Literature

[
33
]

Justice Marvin A. Zuker, in
Children’s
Aid Society of Toronto v. Sheila Ann C.
, [2005] O.J. No. 2154, 143
A.C.W.S. (3d) 869, [2005] W.D.F.L. 3688,
2005 ONCJ 274
, 2005 Cars­well­Ont 2424
(Ont. C.J.),
[1]

provided an excellent review of the insidious impact of domestic violence on
women and children, which includes references to various social science materials.
Some excerpts are as follows (my emphasis added):

[86]
The
gravity, indeed, the tragedy of domestic violence can hardly be overstated.
Expert testimony on the psychological effects of battering have been admitted
in American courts in recent years.  . . .

[87]
The
cycle of violence conforms to the Walker “cycle theory of violence” named for clinical psychologist Dr.
Lenore E. Walker, the pioneer researcher in the field of the battered wife syndrome.
Dr. Walker first described the cycle in the book
The Battered Woman
,
(New York: Harper Colophon Books, 1979).  In her 1984 book,
The Battered
Woman Syndrome
, 2nd ed. (New York: Springer Publishing Co., 2000).  Dr. Walker reported the results
of a study involving 400 battered women.  Her research was designed to test
empirically the theories expounded in her earlier book.

The tension reduction theory states that
there are three distinct phases associated in a recurring battering cycle:
(1) tension building, (2) the acute battering incident, and (3) loving contrition.
During the first phase, there is a gradual escalation of tension displayed by
discrete acts causing increased friction such as name-calling, other mean
intentional behaviours, and/or physical abuse.  The batterer expresses
dissatisfaction and hostility but not in an extreme or maximally explosive
form.  The woman attempts to placate the batterer, doing what she thinks
might please him, calm him down, or at least, what will not further aggravate
him.  She tries not to respond to his hostile actions and uses general anger reduction
techniques.  Often she succeeds for a little while which reinforces her
unrealistic belief that she can control this man  . . .

[88]
The
tension continues to escalate and eventually she is unable to continue
controlling his angry response pattern.  “Exhausted from the constant stress,
she usually withdraws from the batterer, fearing she will inadvertently set
off an explosion.  He begins to move more oppressively toward her as he
observes her withdrawal.  . . .  Tension between the two
becomes unbearable” (Walker, 1979, page 59).  The second phase, the acute
battering incident, becomes inevitable without intervention.  Sometimes, she
precipitates the inevitable explosion so as to control where and when it
occurs, allowing her to take better precautions to minimize her injuries and
pain.

[89]
“Phase
two is characterized by the uncontrollable discharge of the tensions that
have built up during phase one” (Walker, 1979, page 59).  The batterer typically
unleashes a barrage of verbal and physical aggression that can leave the
woman severely shaken and injured.  In fact, when injuries do occur, it
usually happens during this second phase.  It is also the time that police
become involved, if they are called at all.  The acute battering phase is
concluded when the batterer stops, usually bringing with its cessation a
sharp physiological reduction in tension.  This in itself is naturally
reinforcing.  Violence often succeeds because it does work.

[90]
In
Dr. Walker’s “phase three” which follows, the batterer may apologize
profusely, try to assist his victim, show kindness and remorse and shower her
with gifts and/or promises.  The batterer himself may believe at this point
that he will never allow himself to be violent again.  The woman wants to
believe the batterer and, early in the relationship at least, may renew her
hope in his ability to change.  This third phase provides, for the woman, the
positive reinforcement for remaining in the relationship.  In fact, results
showed that phase three could also be characterized by an absence of tension
or violence and no observable loving-contrition behaviour, and still be
reinforcing for the woman.

[91]
Dr.
Walker defined a battered woman as a woman who has gone through the battering
cycle at least twice.  As she explained in her introduction to
The Battered
Woman
, at page xv, “Any woman may find herself in an abusive relationship
with a man once.  If it occurs a second time, and she remains in the
situation, she is defined as a battered woman.”

.  .  .

[93]
The
partner who becomes battered, if you will, stays in the relationship probably
because of a number of reasons.

[94]
Often
in these types of relationships, the person who beats or assaults, who
batters, often tries to make up and begs for forgiveness.  And this individual,
who basically has a very disturbed or damaged self-esteem, all of a sudden
feels that he or she — we’ll use women in this case because it’s so much more
common — the spouse feels that she again can do the spouse a favour and it
can make her feel needed and boost her self-esteem for a while and make her
feel worthwhile and the spouse says he’ll forgive her and what not.

[95]
Another
manifestation of this victimization is a reluctance to disclose to others the
fact or extent of the beatings.  I find that as a fact in the case of Ms.
Sheila Ann Co., for example, the lack of hospital records does not reflect
the occasions Ms. Sheila Ann Co. attended at hospitals to be treated for
various injuries, but here there was great reluctance on her part to seek
medical treatment, let alone even leave her home which she often did not.

[96]
But
the manner in which she would not tell people about her being beaten was related
to the fact that the whole process would repeat itself.  The abuser or
batterer would want forgiveness and tell her that he would love her and that
it would never happen again and she would feel grateful.  She would feel a
little loved.  It would help her self-esteem again and she would feel a
little safer for a while too.  It would allow her to have a sense, a window
of security for a period because she felt so trapped in this relationship.

[97]
A
related theory used to explain the failure of women to leave battering
relationships was described by psychologist and lawyer Charles Patrick Ewing
in his book
Battered Women Who Kill: Psychological Self-Defense as Legal
Justification
, (Lexington, Mass.: D.C. Heath and Co., 1987).  Ewing
described a phenomenon labelled “traumatic bonding” that has been observed
between hostages and captors, battered children and their parents, concentration
camp prisoners and guards, and batterers and their spouses.  According to the
research cited by Ewing, there are two features common to the social
structure in each of these apparently diverse relationships.  At pages 19-20,
he stated:

The first of these common features is an
imbalance of power “wherein the maltreated person perceives himself or
herself to be subjugated or dominated by the other”.  The less powerful
person in the relationship — whether battered woman, hostage, abused child,
cult follower, or prisoner — becomes extremely dependent upon, and may even
come to identify with, the more powerful person.  In many cases, the result
of such dependency and identification is that the less powerful, subjugated
persons become “more negative in their self-appraisal, more incapable of
fending for themselves, and thus more in need of the high power person.”  As
this “cycle of dependency and lowered self-esteem” is repeated over time, the
less powerful person develops a “strong affective bond” to the more powerful
person in the abusive relationship.

.  .  .

[99]
Spousal
violence is rarely the only factor operative in protection proceedings, but
rather is often combined with a family environment involving other types of
child abuse or neglect.  When there is a high degree of spousal abuse, the
abusive partner is often abusive towards the children and the parenting
capacity of an abused person often suffers.

[100]
In
some cases where the father is abusive to his spouse and children, the child
protection agency may become involved and the agency or courts may allow
children to remain in the mother’s care only on condition that the father has
no contact, or that his contact is fully supervised.  See, for example,
Children’s
Aid Society of Simcoe County v. Donald M., Barbara M. and Richard F.

(2000),
2000 CanLII 22540 (ON SC)
, 9 R.F.L. (5th) 286, [2000] O.J. No. 2159, 2000 Cars­well­Ont 2059
(Ont. Fam. Ct.).  In some abusive relationships, in the pattern of Lenore
Walker’s “cycle of violence”, the abused woman may allow the man to move back
in during his next contrition phase, again endangering children and provoking
the agency to apply to remove the children from mother’s care.  See:

•

Children’s Aid Society of Peel Region
v. Pamela T. and James D.

(1995), 52
A.C.W.S. (3d) 814, [1995] W.D.F.L. 348, [1995] O.J. No. 103
, 1995 Cars­well­Ont
2162 (Ont. Prov. Div.);

•

Children’s Aid Society of
Haldimand-Norfolk v. David C. and Denise C.

(1996), 12 O.T.C. 222, [1996] O.J. No. 3471
, 1996 Cars­well­Ont 3893 (Ont. Gen. Div.); and

•

Children’s Aid Society of
Ottawa-Carleton v. Eve R.

(2002), 112 A.C.W.S.
(3d) 297, [2002] O.J. No. 751
, 2002 Cars­well­Ont 774 (Ont. Fam. Ct.).

In abusive relationships, the
agency should expect evidence, as it did not in this case, that the mother
understands the cycle of abuse and has broken the pattern, for example by
seeking counselling, leaving the relationship and moving into a shelter.  The
mother’s continuing failure to leave an abusive relationship may well be a
reason for making the child a permanent ward.

See, for example:

•

New Brunswick
(Minister of Health and Community Services) v. B.L.

(2000), 95 A.C.W.S. (3d) 314, [2000] N.B.J. No. 67
, 2000 Cars­well­NB
63 (N.B.Q.B.);

•

Nova Scotia
(Minister of Community Services) v. S.Z.
(1999), 181 N.S.R. (2d) 99,
1999 NSCA 155
, 560 A.P.R. 99, 5
R.F.L. (5th) 435, [1999] N.S.J. No. 426, 1999 Cars­well­NS 396 (N.S.C.A.);

•

Children’s Aid Society of
Ottawa-Carleton v. Eve R.
,
supra
; and

•

Children’s Aid Society of
Ottawa
v. R.N.

(2002), 114 A.C.W.S. (3d) 74, [2002] O.J. No. 1562
, 2002 Cars­well­Ont
1528 (Ont. Fam. Ct.),
per

Justice Catherine Aitken.

[101]
In
some situations the concerns of the agency are not limited to abuse of the
mother by the father, but rather it is a violent relationship involving
mutual abuse, often combined with neglect or abuse of children.  See, for
example:

•

Children’s Aid Society of Ottawa-Carleton v. Rachel L.
and Randy L.

(1996), 61 A.C.W.S. (3d) 527, [1996] O.J. No. 746
, 1996 Cars­well­Ont 741 (Ont. Prov. Div.);

.  .  .

[108]
In
the abstract to their article, “When is Domestic Violence a Hidden Face of
Addiction?” by, (1997), 29 Journal of Psychoactive Drugs 337-344, American
addiction professionals, Richard Irons, M.D. and Jennifer P. Schneider, M.D.,
Ph.D., summarized:

Domestic violence and addictive disorders
have a number of common characteristics, including loss of control,
continuation of behaviour despite adverse consequences, preoccupation or
obsession, development of tolerance, and family involvement.

In the body of their work, the authors
continued:

.  .  .

. . .  Domestic violence
and addictive disease will be seen to have a number of common features.
However it is defined, domestic violence involves an effort to control
another person by force, coercion and /or intimidation.

.  .  .

A
number of common features can be found between domestic violence and
substance related disorders. They often intersect with each other to compound
the challenge of effective intervention, complicate treatment of each
disorder, and predispose to relapse of either behavior.  .
. .

.  .  .

Tolerance
develops to not only the threshold for defining uncontrolled anger and
unacceptable behavior, but also the ability to endure physical, emotional,
and sexual trauma and pain.  In addition, the abuser often believes that
increasing threats, control and more severe violent behavior is necessary to
adequately control the victim as the relationship progresses.  Exchange of
pain and antagonistic action is not uncommon as the battering relationship progresses.
Withdrawal is often experienced in these relationships as a period of anxiety
or tension that follows episodes of violence.  Over time the periods of
contrition described in the classic cycle of violence seem to diminish, and
the periods of tension in anticipation of further violence increase in
duration and intensity.

.  .  .

Both
victims of domestic violence and partners of addicts often have difficulty
leaving.  In addition to realistic fears of escalation of violence and consideration
of financial and parenting constraints, both types of domestic partners often
get caught up in a cycle of co-dependency, where they blame themselves for
the current situation and feel that, if they are only able to do particular
things better, the situation will improve.

.  .  .

[109]
In
their discussion and conclusions, Doctors Irons and Schneider commented:

•

Domestic violence is frequently
associated with addictive disorders.  Active drug use is often present during
abuse episodes and, for alcoholics and addicts, maintenance of sobriety is a
key element in preventing further domestic violence.  However, it must be
stressed that chemical dependency is not the cause of domestic violence.  The
drug-abusing perpetrator of domestic violence must be considered to have two
primary disorders, each of which requires separate treatment.

.  .  .

•

Domestic violence and addictive disorders
do not just frequently coexist; they actually share many features.  These
include loss of control, continuation despite adverse consequences,
preoccupation or obsession, tolerance and withdrawal, involvement of the
entire family and in fact of multiple generations and use of the defenses of
denial, minimization, and rationalization.  In both cases it is difficult for
the partner to leave.  . . .

[110]
Evolving
from the belief that alcohol or substance abuse causes domestic violence is
the belief that treatment for the chemical dependency will stop the
violence.  Battered women with drug-dependent partners, however, consistently
report that, during recovery, the abuse not only continues but often
escalates, creating greater levels of danger than existed prior to their
partners’ abstinence.  In cases in which battered women report that the level
of physical abuse decreases, they often report a corresponding increase in
other forms of coercive control and abuse — the threats, manipulation and
isolation intensify: Minnesota Coalition for Battered Women:
Safety
First: Battered Women Surviving Violence When Alcohol and Drugs Are Involved

(Minnesota Coalition for Battered Women: St. Paul, Min., 1992).  Batterers
who are also alcoholic drug users need again to address both problems
separately and concurrently.

.  .  .

[144]
Research
has shown that domestic violence places children at risk of harm on a number
of levels.  First, the domestic violence perpetrator may also be directly,
physically or sexually abusive to the child.  Second, witnessing violence
perpetrated against their mother may have an abusive and detrimental impact
on a child’s development.  Children can develop in appropriate maturity and
sense of responsibility that can inhibit their ability to develop it at an
appropriate level.  Third, a perpetrator may abuse a child as part of the violence
against their partner.  Fourth, children can feel guilty, blame themselves
and feel depressed.  Fifth, children can develop fears, insecurity and low
self esteem as a result of witnessing domestic violence.  Finally,
children
can suffer emotional confusion that can result in bedwetting, nightmares,
sleeping or eating disturbances, self-harm and weight loss.
I have
absolutely no doubt that this child is likely to suffer significant harm
unless I make the order that the society is seeking.

[
34
]

In my decision,
Children’s
Aid Society of Algoma v. P. (Deborah) and L. (Henry)
,
2006 ONCJ 170
, 28
R.F.L. (6th) 372, [2006] O.J. No. 1878, 2006 Cars­well­Ont 2974 (Ont. C.J.), I
stated (emphasis added):

[79]
. . .

It is well accepted
that, even if there is no direct violence to children in a family context,
the continuous exposure to domestic violence among the adults in the family
unit may have an impact on the healthy emotional development of children.
Aside from the emotional impact on children as they grow into adults, the exposure
to domestic violence is often related to the violent and angry behaviour of
children who end up in the youth criminal justice system and eventually as
adults in the adult criminal justice system.

4:     ANALYSIS

[
35
]

The mother’s plan is to return the children
to her under terms and conditions of a twelve-month supervision order.  She
will continue with the domestic violence counselling that began seven weeks
before the trial.  She strongly says that she will abide by a no-contact order
with the father.  If necessary, if the father comes around, she will call the
police and the society.  She promises complete co-operation with the society.

[
36
]

Her main argument is her progress to date
has been an evolution.  She had significant addiction issues.  There were
parenting deficits.  She has taken extensive programming to resolve those two
areas and has made substantial progress.  Because she has demonstrated a
positive disposition towards counselling in general, she is a good candidate
for successful domestic violence counselling.  She further argues there is no
evidence that she has allowed the father to have access to the children when she
has had unsupervised access.  (About one-quarter of the total access of the
mother was unsupervised.  Eventually, all of her access became supervised
because of the risk of her allowing the father access to the children and thus
circumventing his supervised access).

[
37
]

For the two older children, I only have two
choices.  The children must be made Crown wards or returned to their mother
under a supervision order.  For the youngest child, it is still open to order a
brief period of society wardship.  (The youngest child would be in care one
year as of 8 April 2009).

[
38
]

The most significant term of any supervision
order would be no contact between the mother and father.  Is it reasonable to
expect the mother to abide by such an order?  Is it reasonable for the society
to work with the mother alone, as opposed to working with the parents together?

[
39
]

Ideally, a rehabilitation plan should
involve integration of the children with both parents.  Such is not feasible in
this case.  The father has not filed pleadings and participated in the legal
process.  He has not co-operated with the society as to rehabilitation programs.
His limited involvement has been to arrange and participate in access.  The father’s
position has forced the society to deal with the mother alone.

[
40
]

It is not realistic to expect the father, on
his own volition, to stay away from the mother.  Unfortunately, his perception
of the criminal justice system is that there are only minor consequences to
repeated assaults on the same victim.  The three assaults led to three probation
orders.  There were countless breaches of the first two probation orders
wherein there was a complete bar to associating or communicating with the
mother.  In the third probation order, modified contact was allowed.  He
ignored this carrot and continued to have extensive contact with the mother
outside of the allowable periods of contact.  It is reasonable to expect that
he will continue to initiate contact with the mother.

[
41
]

Because of the real likelihood that the
father will seek out contact with the mother and the children, can the mother
protect herself and the children, by resisting the father’s initiatives?  In
assessing the mother’s ability to terminate any kind of relationship with the father,
I must examine her actions, not her words.  Her strong opinion and desire to
abide by a no-contact term in a supervision order is of little value.

[
42
]

A factor to be considered is the mother’s
different presentation in the child protection system and the criminal justice
system.  In the child protection system, her plan is clear; to terminate all
involvement with the father.  The society’s expectation on this issue has been
known by the mother for over two years.  It has been clear and consistent.  The
mother must make a clear break from the father in order to resume care of the
children.

[
43
]

In the criminal justice system, the mother
has repeatedly made it clear that she wanted to reconcile and re-cohabit with
the father.  She has fought to ensure that he has obtained bail.  Her strong
view has been that he not be incarcerated on any of his sentences.

[
44
]

Her actions at the sentence hearing on 21
April 2008 demonstrate her real feelings — she wants to reconcile and
re-cohabit.  She participated in a sentencing process wherein she knew
misleading information was being provided to the sentencing judge.  She made it
clear in her evidence in this proceeding that she did not agree with the
purported changes to the father being advanced during argument.  She also
indicates in this hearing that she was aware of such, as she sat in court
during the sentence hearing.

[
45
]

A review of the transcript of the sentence
hearing indicates the following.  The father stated to the court:

I just want to — me and [Ms. T.S.] to
work on our relationship and I want to do couples counselling, but I want to
get my own place until CAS approves that — that if we’ll [
sic
] go back
with her and the kids whenever she gets them back.

The sentencing judge
indicated (my emphasis added):

What he [the father] says makes a great
deal of sense, of course, and it is supported by the matters that are set out
in the pre-sentence report.  . . .  The submissions made
by counsel reflecting [Mr. P.T.’s] “progress” is a word that Mr. Toffoli [the
father’s counsel] uses in describing the completion of the Pinegate program
and the PARS program [P.A.R.S. = Partner Assault Response Program] and the
Jubilee Centre program in Timmins.  . . .  A domestic
situation coming before the courts for a third time normally would result in
a straight jail term.  . . .  Now, what is different
about this situation today is that [Mr. P.T.] has made significant strides in
taking some control and determination of his own life and giving it some
direction.  . . .  the materials that are presented to me
indicate that his lady wishes there could be some form of reconciliation.
It
has always been my view that the primary concern is the relationship and, if
there is good in the relationship, that it ought to be fostered and
continued,
particularly when there are children involved.  . . .
As I read the pre-sentence report,
I glean that the relationship is
worth protecting and salvaging,
but that the relationship to be
restored will be for these persons a learned behaviour.  [Mr. P.T.] has
demonstrated that he is capable of learned behaviour in the matters that I
have already referred to.  The indication that I get from the pre-sentence
report that, if these persons had limited contact with each other, then
learned behaviour may well evolve into a more sustaining relationship between
them.  That becomes particularly significant when I consider that these
persons have brought three lives into being, one very recently, and that
these
children deserve  parents in relationship with each other and with them,

if possible.  The children’s aid society has taken the children into its care
and custody, and that is a good thing because that is where the children
ought to be until [Mr. P.T.] and his lady have demonstrated that they are
capable of developing their relationship into a secure and lasting one for
their own benefit and the benefit of their children.
. . .  the footprints lefts in the winter snow are that
there are good strides being taken to develop a relationship that can be
meaningful for the community and that, that ought to be given a priority as
an appropriate sentencing consideration.

[
46
]

The criminal court was clearly sanctioning a
probation plan that encouraged reconciliation and re-cohabiting, so much so
that the previous no-contact order was modified to allow limited contact during
fixed periods of time and in public places.  This was intended to allow the
mother and father some legal contact so such could be used as a building block
toward ultimate reconciliation.  The mother made it clear in the pre-sentence
report that she wanted the relationship salvaged.

[
47
]

The mother is internally conflicted as to
what she wants.  Historically, in the child protection context, she has
demonstrated denial and minimization of the father’s behaviour, which is
typical of female victims of domestic violence.  Over time, she has developed
some rational understanding as to the risks that he poses to herself and the
children.  She has come to realize, to some extent, that reconciliation is not
realistic.  I found her evidence fascinating in this regard.  She can detach
and analyze her own feelings at the criminal sentence hearing and recognize
what was being said was wrong or not realistic.  She is in a continuous struggle
with her rational side and emotional side.  She still cannot reconcile the
two.  Had the sentencing judge been aware of her thoughts at the time and her
evidence in this hearing, the criminal sentencing may have had a different
outcome.  What is important is that the mother suppressed her sceptical views
as to changes.

[
48
]

This internal struggle between the emotional
and rational leaves her with a poor defence mechanism to prevent communication
with the father.  She will likely give in to him.  Despite the olive branch
held out by the criminal court, they continued to have extensive access with
each other outside of the permissible times.  The message is court orders mean
little, not only to the father, but also to the mother.  If she breaks the
criminal court order with impunity (including conceiving the third child), she
will likewise break a no-contact provision in a supervision order.

[
49
]

Another factor in assessing the mother’s
capability of disengaging from contact or communication with the father is her
appreciation, or lack thereof, of the assaultive history.  Again, I see this
conflict on two levels.  At times, there is denial and minimization, then there
is rational understanding of the risks that he poses to herself and the
children.  She cannot resolve the two.

[
50
]

In order to have an understanding where the
mother is
really
at, during the time period of this trial, it is
important to look at the so-called Timmins incident.  The mother denies that she was with the father and
denies receiving the black eye from the father.

[
51
]

There are two things we know for sure.
First, the mother was assaulted by somebody.  Second, we know the mother lied
to the society when she gave her initial explanation to the social worker that
it was her sister’s boyfriend who assaulted her.

[
52
]

She explained in her trial evidence that she
was not assaulted by the sister’s boyfriend but was in fact assaulted by two
girls with whom she had an altercation.  She explains this different version at
trial on the basis she did not want the social worker to know that she had an
alcohol relapse at the time of the incident.  She could not explain why the two
different versions of how she was assaulted had anything to do with the
covering up of the alcohol relapse, wherein she drank to the point where she
was drunk.  Her answers on this point were illogical.

[
53
]

The mother concedes to not telling the
truth.  Was she assaulted by the sister’s boyfriend or two other females who
were complete strangers?  I am sceptical of either the explanation to the
social worker or the evidence at trial.  Both versions are probably false.

[
54
]

The mother had a way out of her dilemma.
The society approached the father in mid-June 2008 and requested either a
consent or a letter from the father’s employer that would corroborate the
father’s version that he worked an extra few days and therefore could not have
been in Timmins at the same
time as the mother.  The father did not provide the letter.  The mother was
aware of this and she did not request the father to provide the letter.  Had
they been telling the truth, the letter would have been perfect corroboration,
removing the father completely from the context and leading to the conclusion
she was assaulted by somebody other than the father.  The failure to obtain the
letter, along with all of the other circumstances, lead to an inescapable
conclusion.  I am satisfied that it is more probable than not that the father
was the one who assaulted the mother in the mid-June 2008 incident.

[
55
]

Why has the mother so strongly denied the
father was the cause of the June 2008 assault?  I suspect there are two
reasons.  First, the internal conflict between the rational and emotional makes
it difficult for her to accept the pattern of repeated assaults.  It is a feature
of a domestic violence victim that he or she either denies or minimizes.
Second, the mother must have known how much was at stake if there was a
provable assault in mid-June 2008.  In a child protection context. this would
have meant that an assault took place some three months before trial.  She
wants to distance the last assault as far away from the trial as possible.

[
56
]

In the criminal justice context, she also
had to have known the high stakes.  The sentencing judge in April 2008 strongly
warned the father of any further assaultive behaviour.  The mother had to have
known that, if there was a fourth conviction for assault, the father would not
have obtained bail and almost certainly would have been incarcerated as part of
the penalty.  She misled the society in her June statement and again misled the
court in this trial; all of this was done to protect the father.

[
57
]

The Timmins incident demonstrates the deceitful and denial features of the domestic
violence victim.  This leads to going back to the abuser time and time again.
She is not capable of resisting his initiatives for contact or for that matter,
her own. She is not likely to report either contact or assaultive behaviour,
which would be an expectation of any supervision order.

[
58
]

Another factor in assessing the mother’s
capacity to extricate herself from the father, is her understanding of the
relationship between addictions and domestic violence.  She gave conflicting
and confusing answers as to the relationship between his alcohol consumption
and domestic violence.  She seems to suggest he is at less risk if he is sober.
She does not understand the social science literature as to how addictions and
domestic violence intersect.  Although the two are often wrapped up together,
the
absence of alcohol or drugs does not lower the risk of violence.
The
alcoholic problem is a stand-alone disorder from the domestic violence disorder.

Research has shown that, if the alcoholic disorder has been resolved or
if the person goes through periods of sobriety, he or she is not at less risk
for perpetrating violence.
Each of these disorders requires separately
focused therapy.

[
59
]

Without this understanding, the mother will
be lulled into a sense of complacency if the father presents himself as sober.
She will see this as less threatening.  In examining the history of this
couple, there is at least one assault wherein the father was sober and there
were other instances of an angry, volatile context, wherein there was no direct
physical assault, but again in circumstances wherein he was sober.  This father
is not less menacing because he is sober.  The mother does not have a good
grasp of this concept.  If the children are with her in their residence and the
father shows up in a sober state, the mother is likely to allow him access to
the home and children.

[
60
]

Some of the mother’s answers demonstrate her
confusion and lack of appreciation of her own internal responses.  Some
examples are:

Q:

When you say he’s unhealthy, what did you
mean?

A:

That he’s drinking and just not doing
what he needs to be doing, counselling.

Q:

So, I guess the question that we all
probably have is that, given that you know or you’ve told us that you think
[Mr. Patrick T’s] unhealthy, why have you continued to have any contact with
him?

A:

Our kids, just to keep him updated.

Q:

Do you realize that there are other ways
that he could be updated with respect to the children?

A:

Yes.

Q:

So given that, why have you continued to
have contact with him?

A:

I don’t know really.

.  .  .

Q:

This is the man that assaulted you in
December the 21st ’07, when you were approximately four or five months
pregnant with [S.T.C.]?

A:

Yes.

Q:

And he knew that you were carrying his
child?

A:

Yes.

Q:

And this character slapped and hit you to
the point where you fell to the ground, is that right?

A:

Yes.

Q:

And you still have contact with him,
right?

A:

Yes.

Q:

And you were in court supporting him,
right?

A:

Yes.

Q:

Is there something wrong with this
picture, Ms. [T.S.]?

A:

Yes.

.  .  .

Q:

Okay, so when Mr. Toffoli [counsel for
the father in the sentence hearing of 21 April 2008] is up there telling all
these nice things to the judge, they were wrong then, is that correct?

A:

Yes.

Q:

Why were you there supporting him?

A:

I don’t know, we have a son
together, a newborn.

.  .  .

Q:

You knew that the children’s aid society,
their expectations, you’ve already admitted, absolutely no contact, is that
right?

A:

Yes.

Q:

How did he get to your home, how did he
get inside your home for two hours, how did that happen?

A:

Well he was walking around, he was saying
he couldn’t look for a place to stay before that  . . .

Q:

Say it again, please?

A:

He couldn’t look for a place to stay, he
was staying in a tent with his friend Andy.

Q:

Yes, go ahead.

A:

And he came over and then he asked if I
can come in and I said “Yes, okay, just for a little while.” and then we were
talking and, I don’t know, I must have lost track of time.

Q:

During the time that he arrived at the
house and the time that he left, did you ever ask him to leave?

A:

Yes.

Q:

Oh, you did, and what did he say?

A:

He’s like, “Yes, I’ll go soon, I just
want to make a quick phone call.”

Q:

You knew what the society’s expectations
were, no contact whatsoever?

A:

Yes.

Q:

Why would you allow this man in your home
for two seconds?  Answer that, tell the court that.

A:

Because I’m, I don’t know, I’m kind of
depressed and he’s the only person I know in Sudbury.

Q:

The simple hard fact is, and it might be
gone by the time your counselling is finished, [Ms. T.S.],
but the
simple hard fact is, you’ve still got, to a certain extent, a dependant
relationship upon [Mr. P.T.], isn’t that a fact?

A:

Yes.

Q:

Pardon me?

A:

Yes.

[
61
]

If these children were sent home under a
supervision order, there would have to be the immediate termination of contact
between the mother and father.  That is unrealistic.  The mother and father
have developed over a lengthy period of time a casual and comfortable relationship,
so much so, that they breach probation orders, giving little if any thought to
compliance.  In the incident of 26 August 2008, wherein the father spent time
at the mother’s residence, this was two weeks before the commencement of the
trial.  How could the mother be so brazen to risk getting caught so close to a
trial wherein her plan is termination of contact with the father?  It is
because they are so casual in getting together that they are oblivious to
consequences.  I do not believe the mother when she says the father was out for
an early morning stroll and came over to her house at 6:45 a.m.  He probably
did spend the night at her residence; after all, he was living in a tent at
that time.  Again on 8 September 2008, two days before the commencement of the
trial, she is with the father.  If the children were returned, she would not
refrain from contact with the father, except perhaps for a short period of
time.

[
62
]

Counsel for the mother argues there is no
evidence that the mother has allowed the father to have access to the children
or to herself during the period of time of the mother’s unsupervised access.
Therefore, it can be inferred, the mother has kept the father away from herself
and the children.  I am not prepared to draw that inference.  This couple have
had substantial clandestine access to each other.  I doubt that their access
has been limited to all the times when they have been caught.

[
63
]

On examining the features in the social
science literature, and examining the mother’s history, it is evident she
demonstrates many of these features.  Two things strike me.  First, the victim has
a sense of powerlessness and is controlled like a remote control car.  Second,
a victim cannot escape this cycle without significant therapy.  One thing is
clear — a woman cannot overcome this cycle by sheer force of personal will,
which is what the mother is primarily relying on to keep the father at a distance.

[
64
]

The mother commenced counselling with Julie
LeBreton of the domestic violence and sexual assault treatment program at the Sudbury Regional
Hospital.  As of the time of trial, she had three to four
sessions.  Ms. LeBreton points out (my emphasis added):

I believe that the extent and
complexity of [Ms. T.S.’s] trauma has been underestimated and as such under
treated.
[Ms. T.S.] has disclosed that both
of her parents were survivors (her mother is now deceased) of the Residential
School Regime and it has become apparent to me that [Ms. T.S.] is also a
victim of the intergenerational transmission of trauma.  There is a lengthy
list of impacts that Intergenerational Survivors face including
. . .  Alcohol and drug abuse; Sexual abuse; Physical
abuse  . . .  Psychological/emotional abuse; Low
self-esteem; Dysfunctional families and interpersonal relationships;
Parenting issues..Depression  . . .  anger
. . .

It is clear to me that [Ms. T.S.] is a woman
of tremendous fortitude for there are few of us who could have endured her
life and still continued to struggle to improve our well being.  More than
just surviving, [Ms. T.S.] is a uniquely compassionate soul as she has spoken
out on many occasions of her longing to see better in the world
. . .  This can be noted therapeutically as a sign of
her ability to heal herself.

Despite repeated early trauma and
continuous abuse from multiple persons, [Ms. T.S.] continues to demonstrate
emotional progression and a willingness for self-responsibility.
Therapeutically it is known that the capacity for self reflection is
contingent upon safety and this has been a barrier for [Ms. T.S.] but has
stated that she is ready to heal  . . .
The extent
of time is unclear but progress should be continual and able to be observed.

[Ms. T.S.] requires workers who have
specific knowledge of PTSD [Post Traumatic Stress Disorder] related to
Residential School Intergenerational Impacts — with this in place — I believe
that [Ms. T.S.] has a chance to end The Legacy.

[
65
]

This report suggests that the mother’s
issues are complex and more deep-rooted than initially thought.  The problem is
not simply restricted to being a victim of domestic violence.  There is a
component of Post Traumatic Stress Syndrome and Intergenerational Impacts.  It
would appear she would require a therapist who is specialized in Post Traumatic
Stress Syndrome, in addition to her current therapist.

[
66
]

It is known the mother was sexually abused
in her earlier years.  She has received extensive therapy to deal with those
issues.

[
67
]

The extent and complexity of her trauma is
only now discovered.  It is evident from this report that she requires
intensive and long-term therapy.

[
68
]

What are the implications of this report in
the child protection proceeding?  The lives of these children have been placed
on the back burner for over two years.  This case is yet another example of
serious systemic delay in concluding child protection cases in the City of Greater Sudbury, caused by an enormous
volume and lack of judicial resources.  Systemic delay does have an “up side”,
if you can call it that — it provides parents with an extended time to resolve
issues.  So how did the mother use this extended time?  She has had extensive counselling
and therapy in a number of areas, but the most important risk factor to the
children is the mother’s being a victim of domestic violence.  This critical
therapy only started seven weeks before trial comprising three or four
sessions.  This is a drop in the bucket compared to what is required.  The
therapy started one week short of two years of the children being in care.
There was no adequate answer as to the lengthy delay.

[
69
]

The significant delay in obtaining this most
crucial therapy raises the issue of the purpose of society wardship and
supervision orders.

[
70
]

Society wardship is intended to provide
complete protection of children while parents have an opportunity to resolve
their issues.  Society wardship has a time limit implying that parental issues
should be substantially resolved by the outside of the time limit.  Good
progress toward the resolution of the issues during society wardship should
materially reduce the risk factors that brought the children into care in the
first place, thereby making it feasible to manage the lower risk under a
supervision order.

[
71
]

The legislative intent is that we can only
wait so long to rehabilitate parents and risk factors.  Once the time limits
have passed, then the children must be made either Crown wards or sent home
under a supervision order.

[
72
]

In a high-risk case such as this,
supervision orders are not intended to be the primary vehicle to implement
therapy.  Therapy should commence well before the start of a supervision
order.
It is not the therapy per se that reduces risk to children; it is
the absorption and implementation of the therapy.
Some meaningful
information should be known about implementation, before children are sent home
under a supervision order.

[
73
]

Children’s aid societies do not have the
resources to monitor high-risk cases under a supervision order.  They depend
primarily on third-party referrals and plain luck.  (How else to explain the
social worker’s catching the father in the mother’s residence early in the
morning of 26 August 2008, two weeks before the commencement of trial?)  The
precipitating risk that led to the children’s being in care should be on a
clear, downward trend during the society wardship phase.  It does not mean that
the risk is eliminated, before the children are sent home on a supervision
order.  The challenge is at what point is the risk sufficiently low enough to
maintain it under a supervision order.  If children are sent home without reliable
information on risk reduction, then a supervision order becomes an experiment
to determine absorption and implementation of therapy.  This is not the purpose
of a supervision order.

[
74
]

In this case, we do not have evidence of an
appreciable decline of the domestic violence risk factor.  If anything, the
evidence is to the contrary — the risk remains high, even after a lengthy time
with the children in care.  The mother should have commenced the domestic
violence therapy over a year before the trial.  Then, there would be
considerable time to assess the absorption and implementation.  We can afford
to experiment during the society wardship phase because the children are well
protected in care.  We would then know well before the supervision order phase
to what extent the mother can extricate herself from the father.  Here, the
risk to the children is not reduced and remains high.  It would not be appropriate
to manage such a high level of risk in a supervision order structure.  That
risk is not going to be reduced soon.  It is evident from the report the
mother’s trauma has been underestimated and under-treated.  The extent of time
required is unknown but I infer it will be lengthy.

[
75
]

Domestic violence is not simply about
physical assaults.  It embraces a range of behaviour including mental and
emotional abuse of the mother with spill-over to the children.  The environment
is frequently chaotic, volatile, escalating, charged and degrading.  Exposing
children to such an environment on a pattern basis is devastating to their
development.

[
76
]

If these children are returned home to the
mother, it is very likely they would be back in care soon, setting off another
round of lengthy legal proceedings wherein the children are relegated to the
back burner of foster care.  Already, the majority of their young lives have
been spent in foster care.  To risk further foster care is not in their best
interests.

[
77
]

For the two older children, we are under a
status review application, and as such I have considered the factors set out in
the best interest provisions of subsection 37(3) of the Act, particularly
paragraphs 7, 8, 10, 11 and 12.  The disruption to the children’s care would be
minimal under an order of Crown wardship with no access, for the purpose of
adoption.  The disruption to their care would much greater should they be
returned to their mother’s care and then removed again, which would be very
likely, given the evidence.

[
78
]

As for the youngest child, this is an
originating application and requires a “finding”. The mother consents and there
will be a finding that this child is a child in need of protection pursuant to
subclauses 37(2)(
b
)(i) and (ii) of the Act (risk the child is likely to
suffer physical harm).

[
79
]

For this child, there is still time left to
grant a society wardship order.  I have not been asked to extend the society
wardship time provisions and, if such an application had been made, I would not
grant such.  It is not in the best interest of this child.  It is not reasonably
foreseeable to expect the mother’s situation to change in the near future.  Her
domestic violence issue is deep-rooted and longstanding, complicated by other
underlying psychological factors, wherein extensive therapy is required,
probably for an indefinite and lengthy period.  Her prognosis, because of
coming to therapy late, is unknown and is essentially conjecture.  Primarily
because of systemic delay, these children have already been in care far too
long.  Their lives can no longer be put on the back burner awaiting the
mother’s uneven journey to deal with her risk issues.

[
80
]

Justice Stanley B. Sherr of this court, in
Jewish
Family and Child Service of Toronto v. Rachel K., Tamara K. and Edward King T.
,

2008 ONCJ 774
, [2008] O.J. No. 1940, [2008] O.J. No. 5856, 2008 Cars­well­Ont
9306 (Ont. C.J.), stated:

[67]
The
significance of the child-centered approach is that good intentions are not
enough.  The test is not whether the parents have seen the light and intend
to change, but whether they have in fact changed and are now able to give the
child the care that is in his best interests.  There is not to be
experimentation with a child’s life with the result that in giving the
parents another change, the child would have one less chance.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Winnipeg v. Redwood
(1980),
1980 CanLII 3654 (MB CA)
, 19 R.F.L. (2d) 232, [1980]
M.J. No. 245, 1980 Cars­well­Man 44 (Man. C.A.).  There has to be some
demonstrated basis for a determination that the parents are able to parent
the child without unreasonably endangering the child’s safety.  See
Children’s
Aid Society of Brockville Leeds and Grenville v. C. and J.

(2001), 104
A.C.W.S. (3d) 892, [2001] O.J. No. 1579, [2001] O.T.C. 287
, 2001 Cars­well­Ont
1504 (Ont. Fam. Ct.).

[
81
]

Such a demonstrated basis does not exist on
the evidence.

[
82
]

Accordingly, there will be an order of Crown
wardship for the three children.

[
83
]

Under subsection 59(2), the court shall not
make an access order with respect to a Crown ward unless the court is satisfied
that, the relationship between the mother and the child is beneficial and
meaningful to the child; and the ordered access will not impair the child’s future
opportunities for a permanent or stable placement.  The mother has the onus of
proving both these prongs on a balance of probabilities.

[
84
]

The concepts of “beneficial and meaningful”
have been equated to a significant impact on the child’s life.

[
85
]

The children have enjoyed consistent
supervised access visits with their mother.  Overall the visits are positive
and are enjoyed by the children and mother.  The visits are a small portion of
the children’s lives.  Although the visits are positive, it does not mean that
they are significant.  The mother has not discharged her onus to demonstrate
that access would be beneficial and meaningful to the children.

[
86
]

Ordered access would impair the children’s
future opportunities for a permanent placement.

[
87
]

Because of their young ages and overall
condition, the children are excellent candidates for adoption.  Once a child
becomes a Crown ward, the legislation shifts its focus to permanency planning.
Permanency planning is not long-term foster care; it is adoption.  The mother
has not discharged the onus to demonstrate that an access order will not impair
the children’s future opportunities for a permanent placement.

[
88
]

Therefore, there will be an order for no
access.

5:     POST SCRIPT

[
89
]

In her evidence, the mother read to me a
heart-wrenching letter and made a passionate plea for the return of her
children.  On a personal level, I have considerable sympathy for her.  She has
been dealt very difficult cards in the game of life.  Through no fault of her
own, she has endured several deficits.  She has challenged and done well with
many of those deficits.  There are still serious issues left to be addressed
and I would encourage the mother to go forward and challenge those issues and
overcome them.

[
90
]

Although the mother will be dejected with
this decision, she is still young (24) and has a long life ahead of her.  I
would encourage her to continue the therapy she so desperately needs.  This
should then set her up to make a better choice of a partner in life.  If that
can be achieved, there is no reason why she cannot start another family.
